course.title: Data Science with SQL & Python
course.description: Analyse real datasets with SQL, Pandas and visualisation to drive business insights.

lessons.title: SQL Joins & Aggregations
lessons.body:
SQL Joins & Aggregations

Real data lives in several tables, and joins stitch them together. An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables, a LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills in NULL where the right table has no match, and a CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row (rarely what you want).

Aggregations summarise many rows into one number: COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM() adds them up, AVG() takes the mean, MIN() and MAX() find the extremes. COUNT(column) skips NULL values while COUNT(*) counts every row. GROUP BY splits rows into groups first, so you get one result row per group — one average salary per department, for example.

SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_pay
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
ORDER BY avg_pay DESC;

Step by step: GROUP BY department makes one group per department, AVG(salary) computes the average inside each group, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation — WHERE cannot do that because it runs before grouping.

  • Key points
  • INNER JOIN keeps matches only; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows with NULL for misses.
  • COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) skips NULL.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

mcqs.q: Which JOIN returns only the rows that have a match in both tables?
mcqs.why: INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on the join condition in both tables; the other joins keep unmatched rows too.

mcqs.q: What does COUNT(email) count in a table where some email values are NULL?
options: Only rows where email is not NULL
Only rows where email is NULL
mcqs.why: COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values in that column, while COUNT(*) counts every row including NULLs.

mcqs.q: Which clause filters groups after aggregation, for example keeping only departments whose average salary is above 50000?
mcqs.why: HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation; WHERE runs before grouping and cannot see aggregate values.

mcqs.q: A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders returns which rows?
options: Only customers who placed an order
All customers, with NULLs where a customer has no order
Only orders with no matching customer
Exactly the same rows as an INNER JOIN
mcqs.why: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills NULL for columns of the right table when there is no match.

mcqs.q: What does SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department return?
options: The average salary of all employees
One row per department with that department's average salary
The highest salary in each department
The number of employees in each department
mcqs.why: GROUP BY department creates one group per department and AVG(salary) is computed separately inside each group.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: There are 5 students and only 3 of them have a row in the scores table. What does this query print?
tasks.answer: The LEFT JOIN keeps all 5 students; the 2 without a score get NULL in sc.student_id, and the WHERE keeps exactly those 2 rows.
tasks.hint: Which students have NULL on the scores side of the LEFT JOIN?

lessons.title: Pandas DataFrames
lessons.body:
Pandas DataFrames

A DataFrame is a table in Python: rows are records, columns are named series of values. pd.read_csv("sales.csv") loads a CSV file into a DataFrame, df.head() shows the first five rows, and df.describe() summarises the numeric columns with count, mean, min and max.

Pick a single column with df["age"] — that gives you a Series, one column on its own. Filter rows with a condition: df[df["age"] > 30] keeps only rows where age is over 30. Group and summarise with df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum(), which totals sales separately for each city. Remember the difference between .loc (label-based: df.loc[0] is the row labelled 0) and .iloc (position-based: df.iloc[0] is the first row).

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum())
print(df[df["sales"] > 1000].shape)  # (rows, columns) of big sales

Step by step: read_csv builds the table, groupby("city") splits it into one group per city, and ["sales"].sum() adds up the sales inside each group.

  • Key points
  • df["col"] returns a Series; df[["a", "b"]] returns a DataFrame.
  • Filter rows with a boolean condition: df[df["age"] > 30].
  • .loc selects by label, .iloc selects by position.

mcqs.q: What does pd.read_csv("sales.csv") return?
mcqs.why: read_csv loads tabular data into a DataFrame, Pandas' two-dimensional labelled table.

mcqs.q: What does df["age"] return?
mcqs.why: Selecting a single column with df["age"] returns a Series; selecting a list of columns returns a DataFrame.

mcqs.q: What does df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum() compute?
options: The total sales across all cities
The total sales for each city separately
The number of rows per city
mcqs.why: groupby splits the rows into one group per city and sum() adds the sales inside each group.

mcqs.q: What does df.dropna() do?
options: Removes rows containing any missing value
mcqs.why: dropna() drops rows that contain at least one missing (NaN) value; fillna() is the one that replaces them.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between df.loc[0] and df.iloc[0]?
options: loc selects by row label, iloc selects by row position
loc selects by position, iloc selects by label
loc returns a DataFrame, iloc returns a Series
mcqs.why: loc is label-based indexing and iloc is integer-position-based indexing; they agree only when labels are 0, 1, 2, ...

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
print(df["a"].sum())
tasks.answer: df["a"] is the Series 1, 2, 3 and .sum() adds them: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
tasks.hint: What does selecting one column give you, and what does .sum() do to it?

lessons.title: Data Cleaning Techniques
lessons.body:
Data Cleaning Techniques

Real datasets are messy: missing values, duplicates, wrong types and stray spaces. Start by finding the mess — df.isna().sum() counts missing values per column and df.duplicated().sum() counts duplicate rows. Then decide what to do: df.dropna() removes rows with missing values (good when few are missing), while df["age"].fillna(df["age"].mean()) fills the gaps with the column average (better when you cannot afford to lose rows).

Types matter too: a price column read as text cannot be summed, so convert it with df["price"].astype(float). Clean text with string methods — df["name"].str.strip() removes leading and trailing spaces and .str.lower() makes casing consistent. Outliers are values far from the rest: the IQR rule flags anything below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 * IQR. Always clean on a copy or check the row count before and after, so you know exactly what changed.

df["price"] = df["price"].str.replace("$", "", regex=False).astype(float)
df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.title()
df = df.drop_duplicates()
print(df.shape)  # check how many rows survived cleaning

Step by step: strip the $ and convert to float so prices can be summed, tidy the city names so " goa " and "Goa" stop counting as two cities, then drop exact duplicate rows.

  • Key points
  • fillna() replaces missing values; dropna() removes rows with missing values.
  • Fix types with astype() before doing maths on a column.
  • Use .str.strip() and consistent casing so the same value is not counted twice.

mcqs.q: Which method replaces missing values in a Pandas column?
mcqs.why: fillna(value) fills missing (NaN) entries with the given value; dropna() removes the rows instead.

mcqs.q: What does df.drop_duplicates() do?
options: Removes duplicate rows, keeping the first copy
mcqs.why: drop_duplicates() removes repeated rows and keeps the first occurrence of each by default.

mcqs.q: A price column was read as text like "$49". What is the correct first step before summing it?
options: Call .sum() directly on the text column
Strip the $ sign and convert the column with astype(float)
mcqs.why: Text cannot be summed, so the currency symbol must be removed and the column converted to a numeric type first.

mcqs.q: Under the IQR rule, which values count as outliers?
options: Values below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
Values within one standard deviation of the mean
mcqs.why: The IQR rule flags values more than 1.5 interquartile ranges beyond the first or third quartile.

mcqs.q: Why would you run df["name"].str.strip() during cleaning?
options: To remove leading and trailing spaces so " Goa " and "Goa" match
To convert the column to numbers
mcqs.why: Stray spaces make the same value look like two different values in groupings and counts.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing method so duplicate rows are removed from the DataFrame.
tasks.answer: drop_duplicates() removes repeated rows, keeping the first copy of each.
tasks.hint: Which method name says it drops duplicates?

lessons.title: Visualisation with Matplotlib
lessons.body:
Visualisation with Matplotlib

A chart makes a pattern visible in seconds. Matplotlib's pyplot module draws them: plt.plot(x, y) draws a line chart, plt.bar(categories, values) draws bars, plt.scatter(x, y) plots points, and plt.hist(data) shows how values are distributed. Every chart needs labels — plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel() name the axes, plt.title() names the chart, and plt.legend() explains the colours.

Control the canvas with plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) before plotting, save the result with plt.savefig("chart.png"), and call plt.show() to display it. Pick the chart for the question: line charts show change over time, bar charts compare categories, scatter plots show the relationship between two numbers, and histograms show the spread of one number. A chart without labels is a guessing game — always label axes and add a title.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]
sales = [120, 150, 90]
plt.bar(months, sales)
plt.ylabel("Sales")
plt.title("Sales by month")
plt.savefig("sales.png")

Step by step: the bar heights come from the sales list, the y-axis label says what the numbers are, and the title says what the chart is about.

  • Key points
  • plt.plot() is a line chart, plt.bar() compares categories, plt.scatter() relates two numbers.
  • Always label axes with xlabel/ylabel and add a title.
  • plt.savefig() saves the chart to a file; plt.show() displays it.

mcqs.q: Which Matplotlib function draws a line chart?
mcqs.why: plt.plot(x, y) draws a line through the points; bar, scatter and hist draw other chart types.

mcqs.q: Which chart type best shows how sales change over twelve months?
mcqs.why: Line charts show change over time; histograms show distribution and scatter plots show a relationship between two variables.

mcqs.q: What does plt.xlabel("Month") do?
options: Saves the chart to a file
mcqs.why: xlabel sets the label of the horizontal axis; title sets the chart title and savefig saves the file.

mcqs.q: What does plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) control?
options: The font size of the labels
The width and height of the figure in inches
The number of bars in the chart
mcqs.why: figsize sets the figure size in inches (width, height) before plotting.

mcqs.q: How do you save a Matplotlib chart to an image file?
mcqs.why: savefig writes the current figure to a file; show only displays it on screen.

lessons.title: End-to-End Analysis Project
lessons.body:
End-to-End Analysis Project

A real analysis runs end to end: ask a question, get the data, clean it, explore it, and present the answer. Start by writing the question down — "Which region brings the most revenue, and is it growing?" — because the question decides which columns you need and which charts to draw. Load the data with pd.read_csv(), check it with df.head() and df.info(), and clean it before trusting any number.

Explore with groupings and charts: total revenue per region with groupby, monthly trend with a line chart, top products with a bar chart. When a number looks surprising, dig into the raw rows behind it before believing it. Finish by presenting: one page with the question, three key findings, the charts that prove them, and a recommendation. Keep the whole analysis in one notebook or script so anyone can re-run it and get the same answer — that is reproducibility, and it is what separates a real analysis from a one-off guess.

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df["revenue"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]
by_region = df.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(by_region.head())

Step by step: revenue is price times quantity for every row, groupby("region") totals it per region, and sorting descending puts the biggest region first.

  • Key points
  • Write the question first — it decides what to load, clean and chart.
  • Clean before you analyse; a dirty column poisons every number after it.
  • Keep the analysis in one re-runnable script or notebook so results can be checked.

mcqs.q: What is the correct first step of an end-to-end analysis project?
options: Write down the question the analysis must answer
mcqs.why: The question decides which data you need, what to clean and which charts matter; without it you analyse blindly.

mcqs.q: Which Pandas function loads a CSV file into a DataFrame?
mcqs.why: pd.read_csv() reads comma-separated files; read_excel is for spreadsheets.

mcqs.q: After loading and cleaning the data, what is the sensible next step?
options: Explore with groupings and charts to find patterns
mcqs.why: Exploration — groupbys, summaries and charts — is how you find the patterns worth presenting.

mcqs.q: What does reproducibility mean for an analysis?
options: The charts look the same every time you open them
Anyone can re-run the same script and get the same answer
The data file is copied to two places
The analysis uses only one dataset
mcqs.why: A reproducible analysis is stored as a re-runnable script or notebook, so results can be checked and repeated.

mcqs.q: A chart shows one region with suddenly double the revenue of last month. What should you do first?
options: Dig into the raw rows behind that number before believing it
Delete the region from the data
Redraw the chart with different colours
mcqs.why: Surprising numbers are often data errors; verify them against the underlying rows before presenting.

tasks.prompt: Load sales.csv with Pandas, clean the price and region columns, compute total revenue per region, and draw a bar chart of the top 5 regions. Write a 3-line summary: the top region, the month with the highest revenue, and one recommendation.

tasks.answer: Do it in four steps: load and clean, add a revenue column (price * quantity), group by region and sort, then chart the top 5 and write the summary from those numbers.

lessons.title: A/B Testing Fundamentals
lessons.body:
A/B Testing Fundamentals

An A/B test compares two versions of one thing — two button colours, two headlines, two prices — to see which performs better. Users are split at random into a control group (version A, the current one) and a treatment group (version B, the new one), and you measure the same metric for both, usually a conversion rate: sign-ups or purchases divided by visitors.

Random assignment is the key: it makes the two groups alike on average, so any difference in the result comes from the version, not from who saw it. Run the test long enough for a decent sample — a handful of visitors proves nothing. Then check statistical significance: a p-value below 0.05 is the usual bar for "this difference is probably real, not chance". Even then, a 0.2% lift on a tiny sample is not a business win — significance and size both matter, and you should test one change at a time so you know what caused the result.

control = 100 / 1000 * 100    # 100 sign-ups from 1000 visitors
treatment = 120 / 1000 * 100  # 120 sign-ups from 1000 visitors
print(round(treatment - control, 1))  # lift in percentage points

Step by step: each rate is sign-ups divided by visitors times 100, and the lift is the treatment rate minus the control rate — 12.0 minus 10.0 is 2.0 percentage points.

  • Key points
  • Randomly split users into control (A) and treatment (B) groups.
  • Compare the same metric for both groups, usually a conversion rate.
  • A p-value below 0.05 is the usual bar for statistical significance.

mcqs.q: What does an A/B test compare?
options: Two versions of the same thing to see which performs better
A product before and after a redesign with no control group
mcqs.why: An A/B test runs two versions side by side on comparable groups so the difference in outcome can be attributed to the version.

mcqs.q: What is the control group in an A/B test?
options: The group that sees the new version
The group that sees the current, unchanged version
The group of testers inside the company
The group with the most users
mcqs.why: The control group sees version A (the current experience) and is the baseline the new version B is measured against.

mcqs.q: Why must users be assigned to groups at random?
options: So the two groups are alike on average and the difference comes from the version
So more users see the new version
So the test needs fewer users
mcqs.why: Random assignment removes selection bias: without it, a difference could come from who was in each group rather than the change.

mcqs.q: A result with a p-value of 0.03 is usually described as what?
options: Proof the new version is better for everyone
Too small a sample to report
mcqs.why: A p-value below the common 0.05 threshold means the observed difference is unlikely to be pure chance.

mcqs.q: Version A converts at 10% and version B at 12% on equal samples. What is the lift?
mcqs.why: 12% minus 10% is a 2 percentage point lift (a 20% relative increase, but the lift in points is 2).

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: a is 10.0%, b is 12.0%, and 12.0 - 10.0 = 2.0 percentage points of lift.
tasks.hint: Compute each conversion rate first, then subtract.
